nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $M$ be natural numbers with $M < 3p$, and let $\ell$ be a list of natural numbers (the jobs of one machine) whose sum is at most $M$. Then the number of entries of $\ell$ that are at least $p$, plus the number of entries that are at least $p$ and greater than $M - p$, is at most $2$. Here $M - p$ is truncated subtraction, equal to $0$ when $M < p$. So $\ell$ has at most two entries that are at least…
nodes.title: At most two long jobs per machine

nodes.summary: For every number $m$ of machines, the assignment of the empty list to each of the $m$ machines is a schedule of the empty list of jobs.
nodes.title: The empty schedule

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be a natural number. An assignment $\sigma$ of a list $\sigma(i)$ of natural numbers (processing times) to each machine $i \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ is a schedule of a list $J$ of natural numbers when the sum over all machines $i$ of the multisets of entries of $\sigma(i)$ equals the multiset of entries of $J$, that is, every number occurs in the lists $\sigma(i)$ together exactly as often as it occurs in $J$.
nodes.title: Schedule of a list of jobs

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a schedule on $m$ machines of a list $J$ of processing times. Then every entry $x$ of $J$ is at most the makespan of $\sigma$.
nodes.title: Every job is at most the makespan

nodes.summary: Let $m \ge 1$ and let $L$ assign a load $L(i) \in \mathbb{N}$ to each machine $i \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$. The least-loaded machine for $L$ is the smallest index $i$ at which $L(i)$ is minimal.
nodes.title: Least-loaded machine

nodes.summary: Let $m \ge 1$ and let $J$ be a list of processing times. Let $C$ be the makespan of the schedule that list scheduling on $m$ machines produces from $J$, taking the jobs in the order of $J$, and let $M$ be the makespan of any schedule of $J$ on $m$ machines. Then $mC \le (2m - 1)M$, that is, $C \le (2 - 1/m)M$.
nodes.title: Graham's bound for list scheduling

nodes.summary: For $m \ge 1$ and every list $J$ of processing times, the assignment that list scheduling on $m$ machines produces from $J$ is a schedule of $J$.
nodes.title: List scheduling schedules every job

nodes.summary: Let $m \ge 1$ and $a, b, M \in \mathbb{N}$. Let $\sigma$ assign job lists to the $m$ machines so that $\sigma$ is a schedule of a list $P$ of jobs already placed, let $L(i)$ be the sum of $\sigma(i)$ for each machine $i$, and let $R$ be a list of remaining jobs. Assume that $a$ times the makespan of $\sigma$ is at most $bM$. Assume also that whenever $P$ followed by $R$ equals $P'$ followed by a job $p$ followed by…
nodes.title: Invariant bound for list scheduling

nodes.summary: Let $m \ge 1$. Given loads $L(i)$ and job lists $\sigma(i)$ for the machines $i \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ and a list of remaining jobs, list scheduling returns $\sigma$ at cost $0$ when no jobs remain. Otherwise it charges cost $m$, takes the first remaining job $p$, appends $p$ to $\sigma(k)$ and adds $p$ to $L(k)$ for the least-loaded machine $k$ for $L$, and continues in the same way with the other remaining…
nodes.title: List scheduling from an intermediate state

nodes.summary: For $m \ge 1$ and every list of $n$ jobs, list scheduling on $m$ machines has cost exactly $nm$, in the cost model that charges $m$ for each job placed (one unit per machine load inspected).
nodes.title: Running time of list scheduling

nodes.summary: Given $m \ge 1$ identical machines and a list of job processing times (natural numbers), start with every machine empty and take the jobs in the given order, appending each job to the list of a currently least-loaded machine (the first one in index order), where the load of a machine is the sum of its jobs. The result assigns to each machine its list of jobs. The cost counted is $m$ per job, one unit for each…
nodes.title: Graham's list scheduling

nodes.summary: Let $m \ge 1$ and let $J$ be a list of natural numbers (job processing times). Let $C$ be the makespan of the schedule of $J$ on $m$ machines produced by the LPT algorithm, and let $M$ be the makespan of any schedule $\tau$ of $J$ on $m$ machines. Then $3mC \le (4m - 1)M$, that is, $C \le (4/3 - 1/(3m))M$.
nodes.title: Graham's bound for LPT scheduling

nodes.summary: Let $m \ge 1$ and let a list of job processing times, in nonincreasing order, be the concatenation of a list $P$, a job $p$ and a list $R$. Let $\sigma$ be a schedule of the jobs $P$ on $m$ machines, with load $\ell_i$ on machine $i$, and let $L = \min_i \ell_i$ be the load of a least-loaded machine. Then for every schedule $\tau$ of all the jobs on the $m$ machines, with makespan $M$, we have…
nodes.title: The LPT placement step

nodes.summary: On $m \ge 1$ machines and a list of $n$ jobs, LPT costs at most $n \lceil \log_2 n \rceil + nm$, counting merge-sort comparisons and machine load inspections.
nodes.title: Running time of LPT

nodes.summary: Given $m \ge 1$ identical machines and a list of job processing times (natural numbers), LPT sorts the jobs into nonincreasing order by merge sort and then applies Graham's list scheduling on $m$ machines to the sorted list. The cost counted is the number of comparisons made by merge sort plus the cost of list scheduling, $m$ per job.
nodes.title: Longest processing time first (LPT)

nodes.summary: For a schedule $\sigma$ that gives each of $m$ machines a list of processing times, the load of a machine is the sum of its list, and the makespan of $\sigma$ is the largest machine load ($0$ when $m = 0$).
nodes.title: Makespan

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a schedule of a list $P$ of jobs on $m \ge 1$ machines, with load $\ell_i$ on machine $i$. Then $m$ times the load of a least-loaded machine is at most the total processing time $T$ of the jobs in $P$, counted with multiplicity: $m \min_i \ell_i \le T$.
nodes.title: A least-loaded machine carries at most the average load

nodes.summary: A list $P$ of jobs, machine loads $\ell_i \in \mathbb{N}$ for $i < m$, and a schedule $\sigma$ on $m$ machines satisfy the invariant when $\sigma$ is a schedule of $P$ and, for every machine $i$, $\ell_i$ is the load of machine $i$ in $\sigma$, the sum of the processing times assigned to it.
nodes.title: List-scheduling state invariant

nodes.summary: If $\sigma$ is a schedule of a list $P$ of jobs on $m$ machines, then the total processing time of $P$ is at most $m$ times the makespan of $\sigma$.
nodes.title: Total work is at most $m$ times the makespan

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a schedule of a list $P$ of jobs on $m$ machines, let $p$ and $M$ be natural numbers, and let $d = \max(M - p, 0)$. If every job in $P$ is at least $p$ and every machine has load (the sum of its jobs) greater than $d$, then $2m \le n + k$, where $n$ is the number of jobs in $P$ and $k$ is the number of jobs $x$ in $P$ with $p \le x$ and $x > d$, both counted with multiplicity.
nodes.title: Counting jobs when every machine is heavily loaded

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
